legend: You are given arrays a%%ZSMJ0%%, p%%ZSMJ1%%, and q%%ZSMJ2%% of n%%ZSMJ3%% nonnegative integers each, and a multiset S%%ZSMJ4%% that is initially empty. For each 1≤i≤n%%ZSMJ5%% in order, you then add ai%%ZSMJ6%% to S%%ZSMJ7%% with probability piqi%%ZSMJ8%%. What is the expected value of the MEX%%ZSMJ9%% of S%%ZSMJ10%% at the end of this process, taken modulo 109+7%%ZSMJ11%%?

The MEX%%ZSMJ12%% of a set of integers is defined as the smallest non-negative integer which does not occur in the set. For example, the MEX%%ZSMJ13%% of {0,1,2,4}%%ZSMJ14%% is 3%%ZSMJ15%%, and the MEX%%ZSMJ16%% of {1,4,6,8}%%ZSMJ17%% is 0%%ZSMJ18%%.
input: Each test consists of multiple test cases.
The first line of input contains a single integer t%%ZSMJ19%% (1≤t≤104%%ZSMJ20%%) — the number of test cases.
The first line of each test case contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ21%% (1≤n≤2⋅105%%ZSMJ22%%) — the length of the array a%%ZSMJ23%%.

The i%%ZSMJ24%%-th of the next n%%ZSMJ25%% lines contains three integers ai%%ZSMJ26%%, pi%%ZSMJ27%%, and qi%%ZSMJ28%% (0≤ai≤n%%ZSMJ29%%, 0≤pi≤109%%ZSMJ30%%, max%%ZSMJ31%%, p_i%%ZSMJ32%% and q_i%%ZSMJ33%% are coprime) — a_i%%ZSMJ34%% and the two values representing the probability that a_i%%ZSMJ35%% is added to S%%ZSMJ36%%, as described above, respectively.
It is guaranteed that the sum of n%%ZSMJ37%% over all test cases does not exceed 2\cdot 10^5%%ZSMJ38%%.
output: For each test case, output the expected \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ39%% of S%%ZSMJ40%% modulo 10^9+7%%ZSMJ41%%.

Formally, it can be shown that the exact answer can be expressed as an irreducible fraction \frac{x}{y}%%ZSMJ42%%, where x%%ZSMJ43%% and y%%ZSMJ44%% are integers and y\not\equiv 0 \mod 10^9+7%%ZSMJ45%%. Output the integer equal to x\cdot y^{-1}\mod 10^9+7%%ZSMJ46%%. In other words, output the integer k%%ZSMJ47%% such that 0\leq k \lt 10^9+7%%ZSMJ48%% and k\cdot y\equiv x \mod 10^9+7%%ZSMJ49%%.
note: In the first test case, we include a_1 = 0%%ZSMJ50%% in S%%ZSMJ51%% with probability \frac{1}{3}%%ZSMJ52%%. So \frac{1}{3}%%ZSMJ53%% of the time, S = \{0\}%%ZSMJ54%%, which has a \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ55%% of 1%%ZSMJ56%%, and otherwise S = \{\}%%ZSMJ57%%, with a \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ58%% of 0%%ZSMJ59%%.
Therefore the expected value of the \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ60%% is \frac{1}{3}%%ZSMJ61%%, which is 333333336%%ZSMJ62%% modulo 10^9+7%%ZSMJ63%%.

In the second test case, we include a_1 = 0%%ZSMJ64%% in S%%ZSMJ65%% with probability \frac{1}{2}%%ZSMJ66%% and a_2 = 1%%ZSMJ67%% in S%%ZSMJ68%% with probability \frac{1}{2}%%ZSMJ69%%. So there are four possible outcomes for S%%ZSMJ70%%, each with probability \frac{1}{4}%%ZSMJ71%% of occurring:
So the expected value of the \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ84%% is \frac{0 + 1 + 0 + 2}{4} = \frac{3}{4}%%ZSMJ85%%, which is 750000006%%ZSMJ86%% modulo 10^9+7%%ZSMJ87%%.

In the third test case, we include a_1 = 0%%ZSMJ88%%, a_2 = 0%%ZSMJ89%%, and a_3 = 0%%ZSMJ90%% in S%%ZSMJ91%% each with independent probability \frac{1}{2}%%ZSMJ92%%. So there is a \frac{7}{8}%%ZSMJ93%% chance that we include at least one of them and the \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ94%% of S%%ZSMJ95%% is 1%%ZSMJ96%%, and otherwise S%%ZSMJ97%% is empty with a \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ98%% of 0%%ZSMJ99%%. So the expected value of the \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ100%% is \frac{7}{8}%%ZSMJ101%%, which is 875000007%%ZSMJ102%% modulo 10^9+7%%ZSMJ103%%.
